An "<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">Abridgment</a> of geology," published in 1817, when he was in his ninety-first year, is mentioned as one of his best works; but it seems to have been only a republication or a translation of some former treatise, perhaps the Traité élémentaire. [Philosophical Magazine, Nov. 1817. Monod and Weiss, in Biographie Universelle, XXV. 8. Paris, 1820.] LUCIMETER.—This name has been given to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> employed by Bouguer for measuring the intensity of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> which proceeds from different bodies. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of two lamps or candles <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> near to each other, the intensity of the light may be compared, by comparing the intensity of the shadows of an adjacent body. The shadow produced by interposing the body in the stronger light is darker than its shadow, formed by the interposition of the body in the rays of the weaker; because the first shadow is enlightened only by the light it receives from the weaker light, whilst the other shadow is more strongly enlightened by the light from the stronger light. But this method will not serve for comparing the intensity of the light of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, for the light of the sun so greatly exceeds the other, that when both sun and moon are visible at the same time, the light of the moon is far too weak for any shadow to be formed by intercepting it. For the purpose of measuring and comparing the intensity of the light of the sun and moon, Bouguer reduced the light of the sun and of the moon till the light appeared to be equal to that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>. The eye is able to judge whether or not two lights are equal; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the lights are unequal, it is impossible to estimate by inspection how much the one exceeds the other. Being able to calculate how much he had reduced the light of the sun and of the moon, he was enabled to say what proportion their light bore to that of the candle. For the former, Bouguer, when the sun was at an elevation of 31 degrees above the horizon, received the light into a dark room, through a hole of \( \frac{1}{2} \) of an inch in diameter. In this hole was placed a concave glass to weaken the light, by making the rays diverge more than they would in passing through the hole without a concave glass. He received the image formed by the divergent rays at a distance of five or six feet, by interposing a skreen, which formed a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of the cone of divergent rays: this Lucimeter right section was a round image of the sun, of \( \frac{1}{2} \) of an inch in diameter; therefore the light was diminished by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> \( 11,664 \), since the light received through a hole of one line in diameter was diffused over a circle of 108 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in diameter, and of 116 times the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>. This light he found equal to that of a candle placed at a distance of 16 feet. He employed the same concave glass to receive the light of the full moon; the moon being nearly at its mean distance from the earth, and at 31 degrees of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a>; the same altitude as the sun had in his observation of that luminary. The light of the moon being weak, he received the image at \( \frac{1}{2} \) of an inch from the concave glass, and then the light of the image was so weak as to be equal to the light of a candle at the distance of 50 feet. Now the light of the moon was diminished in the proportion of the square of one to sixty-four, which is the square of the diameter of its circular image. If the light of the moon had been diminished \( 11,664 \) times, it would have been equal to the light of the candle removed to a distance of 675 feet; for as 8, the diameter of the image, is to 50, the distance, so is 108 the diameter of the image when the light is reduced \( 11,664 \) times, to 675 feet, the distance of the candle, which would produce that degree of light. Therefore the light of the sun being equal to that of a candle placed at the distance of 16 inches, and the light of the moon being equal to the light of the same candle placed at the distance of 675 feet, that is, 8100 inches, it follows that the light of the sun is to the light of the moon as 65,610,000, the square of 8100, is to 256, the square of 16. This experiment gave the light of the sun 256,289 times greater than the light of the full moon. Bouguer had results somewhat different from other experiments, and taking a mean of these results, he concludes that the light of the sun is 300,000 times greater than the light of the full moon. The light of the moon, when collected into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> by a concave mirror, which condenses the light into a space 906 times less than the natural state of the light, produces no sensible heat. Bouguer found, by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> similar to that above described, that the light of the full moon, when elevated \( 66^\circ 11' \), was to the light of the full moon elevated \( 19^\circ 16' \) above the horizon, as 2500 the square of 50, to 1681 the square of 41. The sun at the harbour of Croisic in Brittany, where Bouguer made his experiments, has the same apparent altitudes of \( 66^\circ 11' \) and \( 19^\circ 16' \) at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and winter solstices; and he concludes that the intensity of the light of the sun at the summer solstice is to the intensity of its light at the winter solstice, in the above mentioned ratio of 2500 to 1681, or about three to two. He found that the light of the moon when near the horizon, and about to set, was 2000 times less than the light of the moon elevated \( 66^\circ 11' \). This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the light of heavenly bodies, when at different altitudes, proceeds from the want of transparency in the air; for when the heavenly body is not much elevated above the horizon, the rays proceeding from it have a greater distance of atmosphere to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through. than the rays from the same body at a greater altitude; and the rays from a heavenly body in the zenith proceed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a diameter, and therefore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the atmosphere by the shortest path. Bouguer calculates that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of air passed through by the rays from a heavenly body at $66^\circ 11'$, is equal to a supposed mass of air of the uniform density of the air at the surface of the earth, 4275 toises in thickness; and that the mass of air passed through by the rays from a heavenly body $19^\circ 16'$ in altitude, is equal to a supposed mass of air of the density of the air at the surface, and of 11,744 toises in thickness. He concludes that light is diminished $\frac{3}{8}$, or about $\frac{1}{4}$, by passing through a mass of air of the uniform density of the air at the surface, and 7469 toises in thickness. The rays from a heavenly body near the horizon are likewise impeded by the terrestrial vapours, which vary in density, and render the intensity of the light of a heavenly body at the horizon various at different times. The same cause renders the quantity of the refraction of the heavenly bodies at the horizon uncertain. In certain states of the air, the discs of the sun and moon, when at the horizon, appear somewhat elliptic; the apparent vertical diameter being less than the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>. This is occasioned by the greater refraction of the air through which the under limb is seen; which refraction elevates the apparent place of the under limb, by a quantity sensibly greater than that quantity of refraction by which the upper limb is raised. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the rising and setting sun and moon, indicate the greater or less quantity of vapour diffused in the air, and are usefully referred to by the seaman and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> as prognostic indications of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. The existence of a greater or less quantity of vapour mixed with the air is also indicated by the different degrees of intensity of the blue colour of the sky. Some are of opinion, that this colour depends on the colour of the mass of air which forms the atmosphere; others maintain, that it arises from the darkness of space seen through the interposed atmosphere. The blue colour of the sky increases in intensity from the horizon to the zenith, and is particularly intense when seen from the elevated parts of the Alps, because in that situation there are few terrestrial vapours mixed with the air, and it is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> colour of these vapours which renders the blue less intense in lower situations. For the purpose of estimating and noting its intensity, it is compared with different tints of blue painted on a card, as described under the article Cyanometer. See Essai d'optique sur la gradation de la lumiere, par Bouguer; and Voyage de Humboldt—Relation historique, Chap. III. p. 251.

LUS

Pages 605-605

a district in the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol14.html#article-MEKRAN">Mekran</a>. It is of a circular form, and bounded on three sides by an immense range of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is flat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, producing abundant crops of every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grain. There are four passes through the mountains, two of which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINDE">Sinde</a>, one into Mekran, and one into Balouchistan. The present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, Jam Meer Mahomed Khan, can bring into the field 4000 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> troops, and draws a revenue of 50,000 rupees. The different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and districts are governed by petty chiefs, independent in their district, though owning the supremacy of Mahomed Khan. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is Bayla, but the chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> port is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMMEANY">Sommeany</a>. Lus is supposed to be the country of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Oritae.—<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> Gazetteer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Geographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>.

MALUS

Pages 605-607

the discoverer of the Laws of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLARISATION_OF_LIGHT">Polarisation of <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 23d <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1775, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Malus du Mitry, and of Louisa Charlotte Desboves, his wife. His father had a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">Treasury</a> of France, and gave him an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at home in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and in the fine arts; as well as in classical literature, with which he rendered himself so familiar, as to retain many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the Iliad in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> throughout his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. At seventeen he was admitted, after a severe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, as a pupil of the School of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Engineers; and about the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he amused himself with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a regular tragedy in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Cato. He soon distinguished himself in his military studies, and he was about to obtain a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> as an officer, when an order of the minister Bouchotte imputed to him the offence of being a suspected person, probably on account of the situation held by his father, and he was dismissed from the school. He was then obliged to enter the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> as a private soldier in the 5th battalion of Paris, and he was employed in this capacity on the fortifications of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>. Here he was soon distinguished by Mr Lepere, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the works, as superior to his accidental situation; and he was selected as one of the young men who were to constitute the members of the Ecole Polytechnique, then to be established upon the recommendation and under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Monge, who immediately chose him, from a previous knowledge of his merit, as one of the twenty that were to be made instructors of the rest. This body constituted, at that moment, the only refuge of the sciences in France, and the enthusiasm of its members was proportionate to the advantages which they enjoyed, and to the importance of the trust committed to them. In the three years which he passed in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, he was much employed, among other applications of the higher <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, in pursuing the mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, a department of science in which he was afterwards so eminently to distinguish himself by experimental discoveries. He was then, however, obliged to abandon for a time the pursuit of scientific investigations, and he was admitted into the corps of engineers, with the seniority of his former <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the school. He served in the army of the Sambre and Meuse; he was present at the passage of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> in 1797, and at the affairs of "Ukratz" and Altenkirch. While he was in Germany, he formed an engagement with Miss Koch, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> of the University of Giessen, and he was on the point of marrying her, when he was obliged to join the Egyptian expedition. He was present in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>, at the battles of Chebres, and of the Pyramids; he was at the affair of Sabish, at the siege of El Arish, and at that of Jaffa. After the surrender of that place, he was employed in the repairs of the fortifications, and in the establishment of military <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. Here he was attacked by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, and fortunately recovered from it without any medical assistance. He was then sent to fortify Damietta; he was afterwards at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>, at the affair of Ceraim, and at the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>. After the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> with the English, he embarked on board of the transport <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a>, and arrived in France the 26th October 1801. His <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was exhausted, and his spirits were broken, by fatigue and anxiety; but his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his betrothed <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> was undiminished, and he hastened to Germany to fulfil his engagement: his fidelity was rewarded, during the eleven years that he survived, by the most constant and affectionate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his wife; and she died a year <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two after him, a victim to the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which had been fatal to her husband. He had, however, enough of strength and vigour of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> remaining, to enable him, besides the official superintendence of the works carrying on at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> and at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>, to pursue the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of his favourite sciences; and upon occasion of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> question, proposed by the Institute, he undertook the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of the extraordinary refraction of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> crystal, which the experiments of Dr Wollaston had lately shown to agree very accurately with the laws laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by Huygens; and besides completely confirming all Dr Wollaston's results, he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> greatly to extend the Huygenian discovery of the peculiar modification of light produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of such crystals, which Newton had distinguished by the name Polarity, and which Malus now found to be produced in a variety of circumstances, independently of the action of crystallized bodies. It seems <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to suppose that the investigation of the laws of the internal reflection of light, at the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> surface of the crystals, must have led him to the discovery of the effects of oblique reflection in other circumstances; but according to Biot, there was more of accident in his actual progress; for he informs us that Malus had been looking through a piece of crystal at the image of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, reflected from the windows of the Luxembourg, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the Rue d'Enfer, where he lived, and that he was much surprised to find one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> images disappear in a certain position of the crystal; although the next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, at a different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, he could no longer observe the phenomenon, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INCIDENCE">incidence</a>. The merit of his discovery was soon acknowledged by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> as a Member of the Institute, as well as by the adjudication of a Biennial Medal from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, on the foundation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Rumford. It has been thought creditable to the Royal Society to have conferred this distinction in the time of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between the two countries; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> were due for only doing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> conscientiously, it would attach, on this occasion, to those members of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a>, who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> their own optical speculations in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> danger from the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, which appeared likely to overthrow them, at least in the public <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, and who were still the most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in offering this tribute of applause to the more fortunate labours of a rival. Nor was the remuneration of Malus confined to empty honours only; he obtained promotion, from the liberality of the French <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, in his own profession as a military <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and this not for services performed in the field, nor even in a difficult and dangerous expedition to unknown regions, but for experiments made with safety and tranquillity in his own closet. That government had not carried the refined principle of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of labour so far, as to have resolved that all public encouragement should be limited to the precise department in which a public <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> had been performed; and a mark of distinction, which a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> could accept without <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>, was not deemed an incommensurate remuneration for a discovery in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> science. Such a refinement, which has been practically introduced in our own matchless <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, might appear, to a man who had a heart, something worse than sordid; he might fancy that a great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, as well as a great individual, should treat its dependents, "not according to their deserts, but after its own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>:" if, however, a person in office happened to have any thing like a heart about him, the outcry of an indiscriminating opposition would soon teach him to silence its dictates. 1. Mr Malus's first publication appears to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> On an unknown branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, in the first volume of the Décade Egyptienne. 2. He presented to the Institute a mathematical Traité d'optique, before the completion of his experiments on double refraction; it was published in the Mémoires présentés à l'Institut, II. 4. Paris, 1810. 3. His more important discoveries were first made known in the second volume of the Mémoires d'Arcueil, 8. Paris, 1809; and again, 4. in the Theory of double refraction. Mém. prés. à l'Inst. II. a paper which obtained a prize the 2d <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1810. 5. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the measurement of the refractive force of opaque bodies, contained in the same volume, he employs the method, before made known by Dr Wollaston, for conducting the experiment, and computes the forces concerned upon the Newtonian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>; applied, however, in a manner somewhat arbitrary to the circumstances of the problem. 6. Remarks on some new optical phenomena. Mém. Inst. Sc, 1810; p. 105, Paris, 1814, read 11th <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1811. This paper is principally intended to prove that two portions of light are always polarised together in opposite directions, and that no part of the light concerned is destroyed, "as Dr Young had been inclined to suspect:" the author found that light transmitted obliquely through a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> glasses at a proper angle, becomes at last completely polarised. Mr Arago had discovered a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> which appeared to be an exception to the general <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of the polarisation of transmitted light, but it was afterwards readily explained from the theory of the production of colours by interference, as applied to transmitted light. A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, containing the substance of this paper, was published in Thomson's Annals, III. 257, Apr. 1814, on occasion of some discoveries of Dr Brewster, which had been supposed to be wholly new. 7. On phenomena accompanying refraction and reflection, p. 112; read 27th May, showing the universality of polarisation at a proper angle, and examining the effect of a metallic surface. 8. On the axis of refraction of crystals, p. 142; describing an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> for finding the properties of bodies with respect to polarised light, applied to the determination of the axis of crystals, and to the examination of the structure of organized bodies, which appear in general to have certain axes of polarisation, as well as those which are manifestly crystallized. The zeal and energy of Malus supported him to the last, not only in the continuance of these interesting investigations, but also in his duties as an examiner at the Ecole Polytechnique. He died, 24th February 1812, universally regretted by the lovers of science in all countries, and deeply lamented by his colleagues, who said of him, as Newton did of Cotes, that if his life had been prolonged, we should at last "have known something" of the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. (Delambre, M. Inst. 1816, P. XXVII. Biot in Biographie Universelle, XXVI. 8. Par. 1820.)

MALWAH

Pages 607-607

an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hindostan, situated principally between the 22d and 23d degrees of northern latitude. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> it is bounded by the provinces of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AJMEER">Ajmeer</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>, on the east by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLAHABAD">Allahabad</a> and Gundwanch, on the south by Khandeish and Berar, and on the west by Ajmeer and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUJERAT">Gujerat</a>, being in length about 250 miles, and in breadth 150. Till very recently, the whole of this territory was in the occupation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a>, the capitals of Dowlet Row Sindea and Holkar being both in it, and within 30 miles of each other. Malwah is a very elevated region, as numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> have their sources in it, and descend in every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of these are the Narbudda, Chumbul, Sopra, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANE">Cane</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is, however, extremely fertile, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> being in general a fine <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mould, which produces cotton, opium, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and all the various grains of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, besides furnishing pasture for numerous herds of cattle, flocks of sheep, &c. Like <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> and some other provinces, it has two harvests, the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> superior ending in April, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or inferior in October. The tobacco, particularly that of the district of Bilshah, is highly esteemed, and carried to all parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of its produce are sent to Gujerat, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROACH">Broach</a>, or into the eastern provinces, by the rivers which communicate with the Jumna. Bickermajeet, one of the most celebrated rajahs of Hindostan, of whom there is any authentic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, reigned over Malwah; he overran many of the other provinces, and compelled their princes to pay him tribute, and acknowledge him as their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> paramount. Such was his fame, that the Hindoos have adopted his reign as one of their eras. It commenced 57 years before the birth of Christ. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> was situated about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> to the northward of Oujain, and bore the same name. This province was conquered by the Mahometans in the middle of the thirteenth century; but on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Balio, in 1286, the governor Dilavur Khan rebelled, and laid the foundation of an independent <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which lasted upwards of 170 years. Their capital was Mundu, a very extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, situated in the hills, 20 miles south of Oujain. Malwah was subdued, and its capital taken by the Mogul emperor Homayon, in the year 1534, and remained annexed to the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a> till after the death of Aurungzebe in 1707, when it was invaded, and by degrees taken possession of by the Mahrattas; by whom it was divided into several portions among the chiefs, according to the gradual progress of their arms, which has caused such an intermixture of their territories, that it is extremely difficult to discriminate them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> landholders, called Grassiah, still retain possession of some of the hill forts, and exact contributions from the adjoining districts; and a portion of the southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the province was till lately held by the Pindaree chiefs, whose incursions into the British dominions brought on the late Mahratta <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.—<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> Gazetteer, or Geographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>.

MARMONTEL

Pages 607-613

a celebrated French writer, was born in 1723 at the picturesque village of Bort, in the Limousin, in a family little removed above the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of peasantry. Like many other distinguished literary men of France, he owed the early <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> to private <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> and gratuitous public institutions. His parents destined him for trade; but his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> induced him to assume the clerical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and to obtain admittance into the Academy of the Jesuits at Clermont. While there he procured a subsistence, by acting, during his leisure hours, as a private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to some of the more opulent students. He then went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>, where he delivered lectures in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> with considerable reputation, and gained an academical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. His disappointment as to another prize opened for him a correspondence with Voltaire, which finally led to his departure from Toulouse for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he obtained the personal acquaintance of his illustrious correspondent, who at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> extended the most friendly encouragement to all young men possessed of any talents for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. At the time of Marmontel's arrival in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, in 1745, the prizes proposed by the Academy opened up one of the shortest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> to literary distinction, and one eagerly pursued by those who were ambitious of celebrity. Marmontel, like many others, Marmontel commenced his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of letters by gaining a prize for a poem on a subject proposed by the French Academy—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. perpetuated in his successor. But in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> afforded the most ample field for the acquisition of wealth and eminence. All <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> was in a manner forced into that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and was often recompensed with extravagant liberality. In order to qualify himself for dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, he commenced an assiduous study of the best critical works on the subject, which he borrowed from Voltaire; he obtained free admission to the French theatre, which he regularly attended; and he frequented the Procope Coffee-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which was then the tribunal of criticism, and the school for young poets to study the humour and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the public. His first tragedies, Dionysius and Aristomenes, obtained a reception sufficiently flattering for a youthful poet; but they did not keep their ground on the stage; and his succeeding ones, Cleopatra, the Heraclides, and Numitor, had no success whatever. La Harpe, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dramatic critic, condemns them all as bad, except the Heraclides, which he calls a tolerable tragedy of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> rank. In fact, Marmontel does not appear to have been endowed with any talents for poetry, at least of the higher order, either in point of poetical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. It is also evident, from his Réflexions sur la Tragedie, published at the end of his Aristomenes, that he had formed, at least in the early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, the most unfounded and paradoxical theories with regard to the rules of dramatic composition. Hence his plots have, for the most part, but little <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>; his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> is full of puerile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>-places; and his versification is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and constrained. The plot of Dionysius hinges on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> against the Sicilian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, and the love of the younger Dionysius (who, in defiance of all historical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, is represented as a paragon of virtue) for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Dion, whose character is formed on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the heroines of Calprenede and Scuderi. The plots of Aristomenes and Numitor are, for the most part, of his own <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, and are both sufficiently extravagant. In the Heraclides he has followed the well-known tragedy of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a> as his guide. At his first interview with Voltaire, Marmontel had been assured by him, that by the stage he might in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> obtain glory and fortune, and that one successful piece would render him at the same moment rich and celebrated. The prediction was verified; and from the instant at which his first tragedy appeared, he, who had not <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to pay the person who brought <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to his lodgings, and who lived on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> with his baker and green-grocer, was at once plunged into all the bustling intrigue of the first literary circles, and into all the glare and dissipation of fashionable <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. His time was occupied with rehearsals and parties of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; he was received as the favoured lover of the most celebrated actress of the age, Mademoiselle Clairon; and in another intrigue in which he engaged he became the rival of Marshal Saxe. In order to shun the resentment of so formidable a rival, he retired for some time to Passy, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> seat of the rich and sumptuous financier, Poplinière, who had married his mistress, and kept open house for all the idle and dissipated literateurs of the age. By flattering the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> in some occasional verses, which he wrote while residing here, he obtained the powerful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Mad. de Pompadour, who procured for him the situation of Under Secretary of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Buildings. This employment fixed his residence at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a> for five years, which were passed wholly free from inquietude, and are often alluded to by him as the happiest period of his life. The duties of his situation occupied him two days in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, and the remainder of his time was employed in contributing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> to the Encyclopédie, of which his friends D'Alembert and Diderot were the Editors. These articles, which contain many ingenious theories, mixed with strange paradoxes, were afterwards printed together, in alphabetical order, under the general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Elements de Litterature.* Having been engaged about the same time in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> on the subject of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, and searching into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> for the rules and means of the art, this study led him to examine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were true, as was then often said, that all the great strokes of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> had been seized by Molière and the dramatic poets who followed him. In running over the canvass of society, he perceived that, in the inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of follies and extravagancies of all conditions of life, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius might still find sufficient employment. He had even collected some observations to propose to young poets, when his friend M. de Boissi, who at the time conducted the Mercure de France, requested him to supply some pieces in prose, to insert in that literary Journal, from which Marmontel derived a considerable pension. It occurred to him to employ, in a tale, one of the touches of ridicule in his collection; and he chose, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a>, the absurd pretension of being loved merely for one's self. This was exhibited in the first of his Moral Tales, entitled Alcibiade ou Le Moi. The story was much admired, and was by some attributed to Montesquieu, and by others to Voltaire. Its success induced him to write other tales of a similar <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>; and thus commenced the Contes Moraux, which were subsequently collected and printed by themselves. Many of these tales, on which the fame of Marmontel principally if not solely rests, bear reference to the original idea with which they commenced, being for the most part intended to expose some absurdity or extravagance of character. Thus the second displays the folly of those who exert authority in order to bring a woman to reason; and he chose, for example of this, a sul- * M. de Chapsal has extracted from the Elements de Litterature every thing that related to eloquence, and placed the remarks not in alphabetical order, but in that of the subject. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is intended to form a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> of French <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, is entitled Principes d'Eloquence de Marmontel extraits des Elements de Litterature et mis en ordre. Paris, 1809. Marmontel's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a> and his slave, as being placed in the two extremes of power and dependence. In most of them he has reached a very happy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of nature, in the manners and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and it is only to be regretted that he has occasionally thrown a too glittering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> over conceptions of the most beautiful simplicity. As lively pictures of French manners, both simple and fashionable, they are admitted to be unrivalled. The early part of the life of Marmontel was passed amid scenes of rural innocence, with a family which lodged in a cottage, and subsisted by the labour of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; the remainder of his days was spent in the most brilliant and refined society which Paris or the world afforded, exhibiting the most splendid union of literary talents, with all the polish of exalted rank, and the graces of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> elegance. This enabled him to succeed in scenes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which were extremely remote, and, indeed, contrasted to each other—in the delineation of the innocent pleasures of the country, as well as the rivalships, whims, and levities, of gay or splendid life. *The Shepherdess of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>*, which has been the most popular of them all, and *Les deux Infortunées*, are as distinguished for simple and touching pathos as the great proportion are for liveliness. The style is remarkable for facility, and the ease with which it inclines, in pursuing the course of events, to the ludicrous or pathetic. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of M. de Boissi, Marmontel obtained the patent and sole management of the *Mercure*, of which he had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> support. On receiving this appointment, he resigned that which he held at Versailles, and fixed his residence at Paris, in apartments assigned to him in the house of Mad. Geoffrin. He appears to have conducted the Journal of which he had <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> with great ability and judgment. Few periodical works have appeared more diversified, more attractive, or more abundant in resources; and many who afterwards came to hold the highest rank in French literature were first introduced through it to the favour of the public. After he had conducted it, however, for two years, he became suspected of writing a satire against some powerful nobleman. He was, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, shut up for a few days in the Bastile, and on his release, was deprived of his agreeable and lucrative situation. But this misfortune did not discourage his literary exertions. Soon after he had recovered his freedom, he translated into prose the *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>* of Lucan, of which he was a great admirer. He also added to it a supplement, in which he details the events of Caesar's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and concludes with his last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. The French have at all times been great dealers in prose translations of the Classics. But though the shape in which Marmontel exhibited the *Pharsalia* can never convey an adequate idea of the original, his work is more agreeable to read than the turgid poetical version of Brebeuf, by which it was preceded. About the same time at which he completed the translation of the *Pharsalia*, he published his *Poétique Françoise*, containing observations extracted from the various articles which he had furnished for the *Encyclopédie*. It is divided into two parts, the first expounding the elementary principles of poetry, and the second applying them to its different sorts. Being about this period seized with a disorder in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, which had proved fatal to both his parents, he resolved to devote his remaining days to the composition of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">Romance</a>, or fiction of the higher order. The subject he chose was *<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELISARIUS">Belisarius</a>*, suggested to him by a print he possessed from the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of Vandyck. The fact on which his tale is founded was rather a popular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> than a historical truth. But the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> had so universally prevailed, and the idea of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> old man reduced to beggary had been so closely associated with the name of Belisarius, that it possessed all the advantages essential for the purposes of historical romance. In other particulars, the author relied on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and Procopius chiefly was his guide. On its first appearance, in 1767, *Belisaire* attracted universal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> chapters, describing the journey of the old blind <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> to the village where his family resided—his arrival there, and the visit paid to him by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, in his humble habitation, are possessed of an interest almost dramatic, and are composed in a higher tone of eloquence than any thing else which he has written. But those which follow are almost entirely destitute of incident, and are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> so many separate lectures on different branches of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and politics delivered by Belisarius to Justinian. In the course of these dissertations, there are evidently many references to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> incidents, and the system of French politics pursued in the middle of the seventeenth century. The last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> toleration, involved the author in a dispute with the Sorbonne, who published a censure on it, which was opposed by the arguments of Turgot, and by the epigrams and squibs of Voltaire. Though Belisarius cost its author many sleepless nights, he recovered during its composition from the disorder which had excited him to the undertaking, and he sometime after produced his *Incas of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>*, dedicated to Gustavus King of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. Irritated as he was by the recent anathemas of the Sorbonne, his great object in this new romance was to show, that all the evils inflicted by the Spaniards on the Indians had their origin in that fanaticism which he was desirous to bring into still deeper detestation. In Fernando de Luquez and Vincentio Requelmé he has given a sort of personification of fanaticism in its most hideous form, and has contrasted their characters with that of Las Casas, which is intended as a model of the exalted piety and tempered zeal most becoming in a Christian. In the history on which this romance is founded, Las Casas had given a tremendous picture of the atrocities committed by the Spaniards in Peru, and of the sufferings of its offensive inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> of Marmontel had scarcely sufficient strength to paint the determined courage, rapacity, debauchery, and remorseless cruelty of the soldiery let loose on the Indians, nor the desperate characters of the adventurers at their head, who knew no <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and whose sole object was plunder. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> scenes of innocence, tranquillity, and peace, he has been more But he has unluckily abandoned the simplicity, which charmed so much in his *Moral Tales*, for a tone too highly rhetorical; and there is a want of unity of interest from the multiplicity of episodes. The longest is that of the Conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, related to the Inca by some refugees from that country, and who had come all the way to Quito, apparently for no other purpose than to tell their long story. In 1763, Marmontel had been admitted, though after considerable opposition, to the much envied <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of a member of the French Academy, and, in 1783, he succeeded D'Alembert as its perpetual secretary. The situation of Historiographer of France, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">Chair</a> of History in the Lyceum, which he successively obtained, fully indemnified him for the loss of the *Mercure*. He was in the full enjoyment of affluent circumstances, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> felicity, and literary reputation, when the French Revolution suddenly changed the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. During its alarming progress he led a retired life, and though reduced to indigent circumstances, remained secure amid all the violent events of the period. In 1797, he was chosen a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to the National <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a> by the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EURE">Eure</a>, but died soon afterwards, of an apoplectic attack, at his cottage near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEVILLE">Abbeville</a>. Several of his pieces were published after his death. The *Nouveaux Contes Moraux*, which were inserted in the *Mercure*, had been extracted from that journal, and translated into English soon after their first appearance; but they were not printed apart in their original language till after the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a> of the author. This second <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> is inferior in delicacy, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of style, to the former; but the scope and tendency of the stories is more strictly moral. On account of his situation as Historiographer of France, Marmontel had thought it a duty incumbent on him to write some historical work. The period he chose was the Regency of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, which he commenced in 1784; but though he completed it four years afterwards, it was not given to the public during his life. This work is not such, either in point of accuracy of facts, or enlightened general views, as might have been expected from the time occupied in its composition, the materials which his situation opened up to him, or the pompous account which he himself gives of his access to information: "All the great men," says he, "of the age opened to me the repositories which contained documents on my subject. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de Broglie initiated me into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of his most secret negotiations, and Contades traced to me, with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of his campaigns, and particularly of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINDEN">Minden</a>." The most interesting part is the last chapter, containing the relation of some particular incidents which occurred during the regency, as the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, and the visit of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> to France. The Posthumous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Marmontel, drawn up in his declining years for the instruction of his children, and edited in 1804, from a MS. in his own hand-writing, are among the most amusing volumes of the description ever presented to the public. They commence with the author's earliest youth: the portion which comprehends this period of his life is written in the happiest style of his *Moral Tales*, and Marmontel contains many interesting anecdotes of humble innocence, many animated sketches of domestic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, and many agreeable traits of village society. In the succeeding part, the portraits of the most distinguished characters, in the most brilliant age of France, are delineated with so much life, discrimination, and delicacy, and every thing is sketched with a colouring so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and aerial, that the whole representation is exquisite. There is scarcely a single person of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in France whose likeness is not exhibited in this vast gallery,—the pictures of Voltaire, D'Alembert, Marivaux, Thomas, St Lambert, and Helvetius, are all excellent. The society which Marmontel frequented was probably the most refined and brilliant that had ever assembled together; but there was evidently a restraint, a desire of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a>, and want of ease in its intercourse. "Every guest," says Marmontel, "arrived ready to play his part; in Marivaux, impatience to give <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of acuteness and sagacity was visibly betrayed; Montesquieu, with more calm, waited till the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> came to him, but he expected it; Helvetius, attentive and discreet, sat collecting for a future day." Literary fame was enjoyed in France in its greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, but also in its greatest anxiety. Of all the others, Voltaire had gained the most brilliant literary success; yet of him Marmontel remarks, that his glory was too dearly paid by the tribulations to which it had exposed him. It had been said by Mad. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GENLIS">Genlis</a>, that Marmontel, in his *Moral Tales*, showed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the French manners and character, in representing the higher classes, particularly of females, as so voluptuous, and in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> abandoned; but the *Memoirs*, if they record the truth, unhappily confirm his representations. When so much amusement is derived from his minute descriptions, it is perhaps hypercritical to remark, that some petty circumstances, of no general interest, and which might have been better thrown into the back-ground, are brought too much out on the canvass, and are drawn in disproportioned magnitude. But for these details, he states as his apology, that it is for his children he writes the history of his life, and that those things which may appear too minute to strangers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> prove interesting and useful to them. The concluding volume, containing a sketch of the first events of the Revolution, is confused and imperfect. Its incidents were too gigantic for the grasp of his mind, and he appears to have been dizzied and stupified by the rapid whirl and total subversion which he witnessed. An author by profession, the literary character of Marmontel may be fully appreciated from his various and numerous productions. Though he admits that, while he has given the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of others at full length in his *Memoirs*, he has only painted himself in profile; yet from them his private character may be correctly enough estimated. On a review of these, it has been remarked, "That without great passions, or great talents, he seems to have had a lively imagination, a pliant and cheerful disposition, and a delicacy of taste and discrimination, of still greater value in the society which fixed his reputation. Although good tempered and social, he Marinette seems to have been, in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, without heart or affection; or rather the dissipated and sensual life to which he devoted himself after his removal to Paris, appears to have obstructed in him the growth of all generous and exalted feeling. In society he was joyous and easy; gay, without affecting to dazzle; and ingenious, without intolerance or fastidiousness." Maskelyne (Nevill), a most industrious and accurate astronomer, born in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 6th October 1752, was the son of Edmund Maskelyne, Esq., a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of respectable family of Purton in Wiltshire. He was sent at the age of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> to Westminster School, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to apply with diligence to the usual pursuits of that place, until the occurrence of the great solar eclipse of 1748, which made a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on his mind, and which was the immediate cause of his directing his attention to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and of his beginning the study of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> with great ardour, as subservient to that of astronomy. It is remarkable, that the same eclipse is said to have made an astronomer of Lalande, who was only three months older than Maskelyne. He soon after entered as a member of Catherine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, but shortly removed to Trinity. He took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as Bachelor of Arts with great credit in 1754, and proceeded regularly afterwards through the succeeding stages of academical rank in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He was ordained in 1755 to a curacy at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARNET">Barnet</a>, and the next year obtained a fellowship at Trinity. In 1758 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, having previously become intimate with Dr Bradley, and having determined to make astronomy the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> pursuit of his life, feeling its perfect compatibility with an enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to the duties of his own profession. In 1761 he was engaged by the Royal Society to undertake a voyage to St Helena, in order to observe the transit of Venus. He remained ten months in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> prevented his observing the transit to advantage, and the faulty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of the plumb-line of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>, which was of the construction then usually employed, rendered his observations on the stars less conclusive with respect to annual <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARALLAX">parallax</a> than he had expected. His voyage was, however, of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, by promoting the introduction of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> observations for ascertaining the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>; and he taught the officers of the ship which conveyed him the proper use of the instruments, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of making the computations. He performed a second voyage, in 1763, to the island of Barbadoes, in order to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> of Harrison's watches, and to make experiments with Irwin's marine chair, on board of the Princess Louisa, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Tyrell, acting at the same time as chaplain to the ship. The chair he found of very little use for observing the eclipses of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s satellites, and the maker of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHRONOMETERS">chronometers</a> was not satisfied with his report of their performance; fancying that he was too partial to the exclusive employment of lunar observations for determining the longitude. The liberality of the British Government, however, bestowed on Harrison the whole reward that he claimed; and Maskelyne, having been appointed to the situation of Astronomer Royal, and having thus become a member of the Board of Longitude, was extremely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in obtaining a few thousand pounds for the family of Professor Mayer, who had computed lunar tables, and a compliment of L300 only for Euler, whose theorems had been employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. The merits of Mayer's tables having been fully established, the Board of Longitude was induced to promote their application to practical purposes, by the annual publication of the Nautical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALMANACK">Almanack</a>, which was arranged and conducted entirely under Maskelyne's direction for the remainder of his life. He was also actively employed, without any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> than the love of science and of his country, in almost every decision which was required of the Board of Longitude; and he had to give his opinion of the merits of an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fruitless projects which were continually submitted to his judgment. He must of course have made many enemies among the weak and illiberal; but the universal impartiality, and the general accuracy of his determinations, were acknowledged by all candid persons; and it must be admitted that the longitudinal speculators of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> do in general submit to discouraging remarks from persons in authority with wonderful fortitude, and with great personal civility. During the forty-seven years that he held the situation of Astronomer Royal, he acquired the respect of all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> by the diligence and accuracy of his observations, which he never neglected to conduct in person whenever it was in his power, and he required only one assistant. The French had a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> to amuse the public by its exterior magnificence, but the establishment of the observers was never arranged in so methodical a manner as that of the English National <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">Observatory</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their labours were never systematically made public; the attempt which was once made by Lemonnier, in his Histoire Céleste, having been interrupted and discontinued. Dr Maskelyne, on the other hand, obtained leave from the British Government to have his observations printed at the public expense, under the direction of the Royal Society, who are the legal visitors of the Observatory, appointed by the King's sign manual. The early observations of Flamsteed and Bradley were considered as private <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>; Flamsteed published his own, and Bradley's were very liberally bought of his family, and afterwards printed by the University of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, who are still as liberal in bestowing them where they are likely to be employed for the benefit of science. Flamsteed was the Astronomer Royal from 1690 to 1720; then Halley to 1750; Bradley to 1762, and Bliss to 1765, when Maskelyne was appointed. He took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s degree in 1777. He made several improvements in the arrangement and employment of the instruments, particularly by enlarging the slits through which the light was admitted; by making the eye-glass of his transit <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> moveable to the place of each of the wires of the micrometer; and above all, by marking the time to tenths of a second, which had never been attempted before; but which he found it practicable to effect with surprising accuracy, as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the Maskelyne observations at the different wires sufficiently demonstrated. The object of his expedition to Sheallien is well known. Bouguer had made an unsuccessful attempt to measure the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of a mountain in South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and had been obliged to conclude that the mountain was hollow, in consequence of the eruption of a volcano, the attraction being too little sensible. Dr Maskelyne's results, on the other hand, as computed by Dr Hutton, made the mountain more dense than could well have been expected; but those who are acquainted with the difficulty of executing astronomical measurements without an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of a single second of space, will be ready to allow that the deviation of 5" or 6", attributed to the effect of the mountain, is liable to a much greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> uncertainty than the results obtained by Mr Cavendish with the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> invented by Mr Michell. (See Cavendish.) The geodetical operations which were soon afterwards performed with his concurrence and assistance, for determining the relative situations of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> and Paris, were equally creditable to the English artists who constructed the instruments, and to the astronomers and geographers who made the observations with them; and they excelled, even by the confession of their rivals, every thing that had ever been effected in former measurements of the same kind. As no man had done more for practical astronomy than Dr Maskelyne, so there was none whose merits were more justly appreciated. He made every astronomer his friend, as well by his personal kindness, as by his professional labours; and he obtained the rare distinction of being made one of the eight foreign associates of the Parisian Academy of Sciences. His example and encouragement contributed to the establishment of several private observatories, which must always be, if not immediately, at least remotely, beneficial to astronomy, as tending to promote the improvement of instruments, and of the methods of employing them. He was modest, and somewhat timid, in receiving the visits of strangers; but his usual conversation was cheerful, and often playful, with a fondness for point, and for classical allusion. He inherited a good paternal property, and he obtained considerable preferment from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>; he also married, somewhat late in life, the sister and co-heiress of Lady Booth of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>. His sister was the wife of Robert <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Clive, and the mother of the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Powis. He died the 9th of February 1811, in his 79th year, leaving a widow and an only daughter. 1. Dr Maskelyne's first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> to the Royal Society is A proposal for discovering the annual parallax of Sirius. Phil. Trans. L.I. 1760. p. 889. It is founded on Lacaille's observations, made at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, which appeared to indicate a maximum amounting to 8". 2. A theorem for spherical aberration. L.II. 1761. p. 17. Dated from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry, St Helen's Roads: the calculation is adapted to the object-glasses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHROMATIC">achromatic</a> telescopes. 3. The next article, p. 21, is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from Lacaille, recommending him to make observations at St Helena on the lunar parallax, and to remain some time in the island for that purpose; promising, on his own part, to make corresponding observations. It is followed by a Letter from Maskelyne, proposing some additional <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> observations. 4. Observation of the transit of 1761, p. 196. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> was lower than had been expected, and the instant of contact uncertain, from a tremulous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in the apparent discs. 5. Observations on a clock of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHELTON">Shelton</a>, 1762, p. 434. Giving the proportion of .99754 to 1 for the comparative force of gravity at Greenwich and at St Helena. 6. A letter on the mode of observing and computing lunar distances, p. 558. Dated from St Helena: the first demonstration of the practicability and utility of the method. He found the error of observation not to exceed half a degree of longitude, an error which was very strangely suffered to remain as a fair allowance for the uncertainty of observation, in the acts for encouraging the perfection of the lunar tables, only very lately repealed. 7. On the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> at St Helena, p. 586. Observations made in a harbour, for about two months. 8. Note to Lalande, p. 607. On lunar distances and occultations. 9. Rules for correcting lunar distances. Phil. Trans. 1764, p. 263. A demonstration of the rules before published in the Transactions and in the British Mariner's Guide. 10. Remarks on the equation of time, p. 336. Correcting a mistake of Lacaille, and an inadvertence of Lalande, and giving a formula, which, though not geometrically perfect, is abundantly accurate for all practical purposes. 11. Astronomical observations made at St Helena, p. 348. The observations for determining the lunar parallax were too few to afford a satisfactory result. The author suggests, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> might be ascertained by repeated and comparative observations of the apparent distance of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> from neighbouring stars. 12. Observations made at Barbadoes, p. 189. Especially on Jupiter's satellites. 13. Introduction to two papers of Mr Swedon. LVIII. 1768, p. 154. The one on the menstrual parallax, the other on observing stars out of the meridian. 14. Introduction to the observations of Mason and Dixon, p. 270. 15. Conclusion respecting the length of a degree, p. 323, 325. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Mason had been sent with Mr Dixon to observe the transit of 1761, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENCOOLEN">Bencoolen</a>, but their voyage was interrupted by accidental circumstances, and they made their observations at the Cape of Good Hope, with tolerable success. They then proceeded to join Maskelyne at St Helena, and to assist in his operations there. They were afterwards engaged by Lord <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALTIMORE">Baltimore</a> and Mr Penn, to determine the boundaries between <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>; and having completed their survey, they suggested to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> of the Royal Society the eligibility of measuring a degree in the country bordering on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a> and Chesapeake. Their proposals were readily accepted, and the results of their measurement are here recorded. Dr Maskelyne afterwards employed Mason, in his operations on Sheallien, and in computing Bradley's observations, and in improving Mayer's tables, by a comparison with them; but he was so fearful of admitting any empirical corrections, not founded on the most general principles, that he would not allow some of the equations, discovered by Mason, to be intro- Maskelyne introduced into the computation of the *Nautical Almanac*, until Laplace had proved their dependence on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of gravity.
