MORAYSHIRE

Pages 851-852
or MURRAYSHIRE, a county in Scotland. The province of Moray formerly included part of the shires of Inverness and Banff, and that of Nairn, besides the present county; but the name is now confined to this district, which is also known by the appellation of Elginshire. It is situated between 57° 12' and 57° 43' north latitude, and between 3° 2' and 3° 58' west longitude, extending about 40 miles from north-east to south-west, and in breadth from 8 to 14 miles in the interior, but upon the coast from 17 to 23 miles; and it contains, including its lakes, 480 square miles, or 307,200 English acres, of which only about a third is productive land. The county of Moray has the Morayshire frith of that name on the north, Banffshire on the east, Inverness-shire on the south, and Nairnshire on the west. The river Spey, which, with a few exceptions, separates it from Banffshire, is commonly considered its eastern boundary. On the south, it is intersected by a small part of Inverness-shire, by which two parishes, Abernethy and Duthil, partly in this county, are detached from the body of it. It is divided into fifteen entire parishes, and contains part of nine parishes more, the rest of which are situated in the counties adjacent. The Presbyteries to which these parishes belong are, Aberlour, Abernethy, Elgin, and Forres, all under the jurisdiction of the Synod of Moray. The natural divisions are the low grounds which stretch along the coast, varying in breadth, southward, from 5 to 12 miles, and the mountains which occupy the interior; yet the former is not without ridges of hills, of no great height, which generally rise in a line parallel to the shore; nor the latter without considerable tracts of low land, particularly on the branches of the Spey and Findhorn, and the other streams which flow from the south. The climate, soil, and productiveness of these two divisions are very different. The climate on the coast is supposed to be as good as that of any part of Scotland, both in respect to heat and dryness; while the prevailing soil is a sandy loam, in many parts affording plentiful crops, which ripen early, and are seldom injured by bad weather, in the harvest season. The wind blows from westerly points for almost three-fourths of the year. The strong gales are from the north-west, and the most frequent rains from this point and the north-north. Easterly winds, however, prevail in the spring months, to the great injury of vegetation. The annual fall of rain, on the northeast quarter, near Speymouth, is said to be little more than 25 inches; and the medium temperature of the year varies from 45° to 50°. In the mountain district, the winters are long and severe; more rain falls than on the coast; and the labours of the harvest are sometimes not brought to a close till the crops are covered with snow. Limestone, sandstone, and slate, with marl, abound in various parts. Iron was almost a century ago wrought in Strathspey by the York Buildings Company. The rivers are the Spey, the Lossie, and the Findhorn, which receive the waters of a great many mountain streams. The Spey, the most considerable, has a course of 30 miles before it enters Morayshire, at Aviemore, from which it flows in a deep channel, and with a considerable fall, till it empties itself, after describing a line of about 96 miles in all, into the sea at Speymouth Bay. It is not navigable, except near its mouth, and there only for small vessels; but it affords the means of bringing down to the sea the forests on its banks; and the rents of its salmon fisheries, some years ago, exceeded £7,000 per annum. The Lossie flows almost parallel to the Spey, about ten miles distant, and, after a course of 24 miles, during which it works a number of corn mills, falls into the sea at Lossiemouth, about six miles to the north of Elgin. The Findhorn, like the two former, flows from south to north, and enters the Frith of Moray at the village that bears its name, having traversed Inverness-shire, where it has its source, Nairnshire, and this county, for a distance of 60 miles. There is also a valuable salmon fishery on this river. The principal lakes, beginning on the east, are Loughnaboe, which covers about 60 acres; Lough Spynie, which formerly spread over more than 2000 acres, but has been since laid almost dry by drainage; Inchstellie, Lochloy, and Loughnadhur, containing an island on which there are the remains of an ancient fortress, and where it is said turnips have been found growing naturally. Chalybeate springs are found in every quarter of the county, but none of them are in much repute. The valued rent of Morayshire, in Scots money, is £65,603, os. 5d., and the real rent, in 1811, of the lands was £62,312, 9s. 6d. Sterling, and of the houses £2,753, 14s. 6d. In the same year, the number of proprietors was forty-one, five of whom held more than half the valuation and rental; and that of the freeholders thirty-six. Only about a fortieth part is held in feu, the whole, with this exception, and small portions belonging to the burghs, being freehold, but nearly a third is under entail. Many of the proprietors have elegant mansions, of which the most considerable, beginning on the eastern quarter, are Innes House, the Earl of Fife; Findrossie, Leslie, Bart.; Gordonstown and Altyre; Cumming Gordon, Bart.; Duffus, Dunbar, Bart.; Darnaway Castle, the Earl of Moray; Brodie House, Brodie; Grange, Peterkin; Burgie Castle, Dunbar Brodie; and Elchies House, Grant. The size of farms on the coast does not often exceed 400 acres, and the greater number are below 150 acres. The larger farms are generally held on leases for nineteen years, as in other parts of Scotland, but many of the smaller tenants have no leases. This division of the county produces all the species of corn grown in Scotland, with turnips, potatoes, and clovers. In the higher district, barley and oats, with potatoes, are almost the only crops, with small portions of turnips and cultivated herbage, and in some places a little flax. The native cattle have been improved, by crossing them with the West Highland race; and the sheep, which were originally similar to those of Shetland, have, in many parts, given way to the Linton, or black-faced race, and a variety of other breeds from the south. On the small farms, especially in the mountain district, the horses are very diminutive, seldom more than nine or ten hands high; but, upon the larger farms on the coast, they are not inferior to those of other parts of Scotland. In the latter situation, two only are used at a plough, and oxen are seldom worked; whereas, the team in the high grounds consists of oxen and horses intermixed, sometimes to the number of six or eight. Morayshire employs few of its people in manufactures for sale. A woollen factory has been established at Newmill, in the parish of St Andrews Lhanbryd, and in the same quarter another for the weaving of cottons. There are tanneries at Forres and Elgin; and, at the latter place, a tawing work of some consideration, which sends most of its produce to London. The exports are cattle, corn, and salmon, with a variety of smaller articles. The value of the salmon has been stated at about £25,000, and that of all the other exports does not exceed £30,000 yearly. A considerable quantity of timber is floated down the Spey, and shipped at Garmouth; but it is chiefly the produce of Strathspey, in Inverness-shire. The towns and villages are, Elgin, the county town, Forres, Garmouth, Urquhart, Lossiemouth, Bishopmill, Findhorn, Rothes, and Balnatom. The first two are burghs; Elgin is joined with Cullen, Banff, Inverary, and Kintore; and Forres with Inverness, Nairn, and Fortrose, in the election of members for the Scottish burghs. Both these places are of great antiquity. The population in 1800 and 1811 is exhibited in the following abstract. See Leslie's General View of the Agriculture, &c. of the Counties of Nairn and Moray. ### 1800 | HOUSES | PERSONS | OCCUPATIONS | |--------|---------|-------------| | | | | | | | | | | | | ### 1811 | HOUSES | PERSONS | OCCUPATIONS | |--------|---------|-------------| | | | | | | | | | | | |

MUTIS

Pages 871-873

an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Historian, but peculiarly distinguished for the ardour of his botanical researches; was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, 6th April 1732. His parents were respectable inhabitants of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and conferred on him the best elementary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> that could be acquired in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>. His first instructions were received in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of San Fernando, in his native city, from whence he removed to the University of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>. In both these seminaries he was distinguished, as well by his application and talents, as by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of his demeanour. He attended the classical and mathematical course as taught in the latter seminary, as well as to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>; and during his residence there, sedulously applied himself to anatomy, medicine, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. The ardour he displayed for this class of pursuits was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, so that, when he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> in 1757, he had made such progress as to enable him to become a lecturer on anatomy. It was then usual for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of Madrid to select some promising young men, and send them to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, to improve their faculties, and advance their knowledge of the sciences. Mutis was selected for this purpose, but about the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Pedro Messia de la Cerda was appointed Viceroy of New <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, and proposed to the ardent naturalist to accompany him, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of physician, to that interesting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His natural modesty and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of retirement induced him to relinquish the opportunity of visiting different countries, and thereby increasing his knowledge in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and to devote himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of those objects of natural history which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> presented, and which had previously been scarcely explored by any scientific European. He embarked with the Viceroy, and landed at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a> in the year 1760. The various new productions that met his eye at every point in that hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, did not detain him from ascending towards the mountain plains, where at the city of Santa Fé de Bogota he fixed his abode. He had scarcely reached the destined <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his residence, before he began to arrange his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for the collection of those <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> to whose study he was attached, and of which the descriptions formed the delight of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and the basis of his future fame. He soon began a correspondence with Linnaeus, which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> during the life of that celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who procured his admission to the academy at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>. His accuracy, diligence, and enthusiasm, were highly estimated by the Swedish botanist, who felt, in the eulogiums he paid him, that he very imperfectly gratified his own sentiments of respect and admiration.* His skill was speedily known through Europe by all the botanists of considerable eminence, as his discoveries were communicated to many of them, through the extensive correspondence which he maintained.† At the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Mutis arrived at Santa Fé de Bogota, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> was in profound <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of science, and, even in the university, the true system of the universe was so little known, that he is represented as having encountered great difficulties, when he first taught that the world turned on its own axis, revolving round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and was in reality only a planet of the solar system. With the approbation of the viceroy, he began to dispense mathematical, and especially astronomical knowledge, to the pupils in the college of the Rosario; and he had the satisfaction, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of a protracted life, to see a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of scholars formed on the principles of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NEWTONIAN_PHILOSOPHY">Newtonian <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, in spite of the anxious and alarming fears of their parents, who, on its first introduction, considered it impious, or at least heretical. He continued diligently exploring the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a> for every vegetable production, during the intervals of instruction in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and continued both pursuits with unabated ardour. When his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Cerda had finished the period of his Viceroyship, he proposed to Mutis to return with him to Spain, but he was so much fascinated with the solitude of the vast woods and extended plains, with the features of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> displayed on the boldest <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, and the deep azure of the unclouded sky, that he determined, under their favouring auspices, to spend the rest of his life in South America, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of vegetation, and of the starry world. His studies, instead of producing scepticism, strengthened his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and, under its influence, he entered into holy orders in 1772. From that period, he divided his time between <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and the sciences, and, whilst in the former he was a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> virtue, he displayed in the latter the qualities of a genuine <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. It was a fortunate circumstance, both for the science of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, and for the fame of Mutis, that the Court of Madrid felt a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the promotion of that study, and appointed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>- --- * In memoriam Josephi Celestini Mutis, Americae summi Botanici, qui historiam plantarum Americanae, in primis Palmarum, pulcherrimam parat, et plurima nova hinc opuscula communicavit. Lin. Suppl. p. 57. Nomen immortale quod nulla aetas unquam debilit. Linn. † Cavanilles, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, thus expresses himself: "In honorem sapientissimi viri (J. C. Mutis) qui jure merito Botanicorum in America princeps salutatur, debetque etiam inter primates Europaeos colocari." ers in each of its extensive dominions in America to investigate, arrange, describe, and draw their various productions. Mutis was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Botanical Board for the Viceroyalty of Santa Fé, and commenced his operations by the project of that great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> the *Flora of Bogota*, which only the munificence of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> could enable him to undertake. In 1782, he selected the spot most favourable for executing this great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and, judging the central situation of Mariquita, at the foot of the mountains of Quindiu, to be the best adapted for his purpose, he removed thither, and resided in that place for the succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, in pursuance of his plan of study. The place was admirably chosen; for though at the foot of the Andes, it is on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, and in a temperate climate; and, being in the vicinity of the river <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGDALENA">Magdalena</a>, though considerably higher, it has the advantage of easy access to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of temperature, and to all the various family of plants which the greatest possible differences of climate can produce. In this secluded town, he and his pupils were constantly employed in roaming in the extensive plains, penetrating the thickest woods, scaling the highest mountains, and at times encountering the severe <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the valleys, whilst collecting every rarity of the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He there created a class of painters, who drew the plants as they were collected: he had a school of engraving, in which were executed some of those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plates, which have excited so much admiration among the botanists and artists of Europe. The state of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, arising principally from the exertions he made, and the hardships he encountered in these pursuits, induced him to remove from Mariquita in 1772, and fix his residence again in the capital, to which he was also drawn by the desire of being nearer to a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of artists, than could be collected in the retired spot from whence his exploratory journeys had been directed. His labours in perfecting the *Flora* were continued with unabated industry till the end of his life, and after his decease the work was continued by some of his pupils; though it has received serious interruptions from the civil wars, in the course of which some of those appointed to continue it were cut off amidst the contests of the various revolutionary factions. Among these is particularly to be regretted Don Francisco Caldas, who was endeared to Mutis, and most nearly resembled him in his industry, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the study of natural history. Besides the great work, the *Flora*, Mutis finished one on the history of the trees of the quina <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, and exercised his great acuteness in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of the varieties of that family, whose bark has introduced a new era in the practice of medicine. Amidst his botanical labours, Mutis never neglected his astronomical observations and experiments. It had often been suggested by philosophers in Europe, that the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> had probably an influence on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a>, similar to what it exercises on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>. The situation of Santa Fé was favourable for a variety of experiments, which Mutis conducted, and by which he ascertained the fact so clearly, as to remove all doubts on the subject. He was instrumental in obtaining powers from Madrid for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> on the summit of the Andes, at a far higher elevation than any of the observatories of Europe are placed. He had remarked, that the blue of the firmament appears darker in proportion to the elevation at which the observer stands, and that on the highest attainable situations, the sky seems almost <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; so that the stars shine with a brilliancy uninterrupted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and even in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, are visible without the help of glasses. He deemed the position favourable for astronomical observations, and especially for those of the fixed stars; for being near the equator, it commanded a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> both of the northern and southern hemispheres; and from its height, the observer is little liable to interruption from intervening clouds, or to errors from the inconstancy of the refractions. At his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> recommendation, and under his inspection, the observatory was begun in 1802, and finished in 1803. Some instruments were collected in the country, and others were ordered from Europe. The first were, as may be supposed, destitute of those improvements which have been more recently introduced; and it unfortunately happened, that some of those exported from Europe were lost on the passage. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> had not been completed when Mutis died, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> storms which have agitated that country have prevented the completion of the collection. The founder had, however, directed the course of observations to be prosecuted with as much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> as the imperfection of the instruments would admit. Though the wise intentions of Mutis have been delayed, we may hope they have not been frustrated, but may look forward to a time when the catalogue of fixed stars in the southern hemisphere shall be considerably augmented, and their positions determined with the greatest accuracy. In the meantime, some astronomical and meteorological observations have been made and published, in a periodical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, and the exact latitude and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> of the observatory has been determined. Its elevation above the level of the ocean, as determined by barometrical observations, frequently repeated, is 9416 feet. As this observatory is the first erected in South America, as it stands much higher than any other that ever was constructed, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> its advantages shall be properly improved, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be a benefit to science, and a durable monument to the fame of its founder. Mutis enjoyed good health through a long life, which was closed in a manner worthy of a philosopher and a Christian, without pain or struggle, 11th September 1808. He left various manuscript works on plants, on <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">meteorology</a>, and on mining; an herbarium of upwards of 20,000 plants, more than 5000 drawings of plants, and a large collection of woods, of shells, of minerals, and skins of animals. He had also a very extensive collection of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-paintings, of all the various animals of the viceroyalty coloured, in exact conformity to nature. It was the last wish he expressed, that his valuable collections might furnish the basis of a national <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>; but the turbulent season which commenced soon after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and the unsettled state in which public affairs have since continued, have hitherto prevented the fulfillment of his wishes. See El Espanol. Diario de <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SANTA_FE">Santa Fe</a>.

MYSORE

Pages 873-876

properly Maisoon, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the south of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, principally situated between the 11th and 15th degrees of northern latitude, and now surrounded by the British territories, subject to the presidency of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a>. This province consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, elevated 3000 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, from which rise a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lofty hills, containing the sources of many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are the Cavery, Toombuddra, Vedawati, Bhadri, Penar, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of this elevated region is temperate and healthy to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> unknown in any other track of similar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> within the tropics. The rainy season is here more moderate than on either of the sea coasts, but of much longer <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; and during other seasons of the year the verdure is frequently refreshed by enlivening showers. Its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> produces not only all the grains and vegetables of other parts of India, but also many of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The cultivation is also much aided by means of reservoirs and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, from whence the farmers irrigate their fields and gardens. The inhabitants are in general Hindoos; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> having been so often the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of warfare, it is not nearly so populous as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, and some other of the British provinces. It produces horses, cattle, sheep, and swine, but none of them of a good size. This province is divided into three districts, named Fata-na, Nagara, and Chatrakal: each district is managed by an Amildar, who is an officer of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, and revenue, and who is accountable for his conduct to the ministers of the Rajah, who are kept to their duty by the presence of the British resident. As this province is now particularly connected with the British interests, and, from a rival state, is become one of our staunchest allies, it is requisite to enter at some length into its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. The ancestor of the reigning family is said to have been the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of a band of herdsmen, who emigrated with their flocks and cattle from the province of Gujarat, and were allowed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in Mysore. The first person of this tribe who distinguished himself was named Vijeya, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of bravery. He married the heiress of the Wadiar, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chief of the town of Caroogully and its dependencies, and succeeded his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. His immediate successors are not known; but, in the year 1507, Cham Raj took possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, but still acknowledging himself as a subject of the Maha Rajah of Annagoondy, who was a descendant of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hindoo monarchs of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BIJANAGUR">Bijanagur</a>. Tim Raj succeeded in 1548, and annexed some other districts to his government. Heere Cham Raj ruled from 1571 to 1576, and was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> Raj Wadeyar, who appears to have taken advantage of the declining power of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> paramount, not only to annex to his own estates those of the Rajah of Chickraipatam, but to take possession of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and fortress of Seringapatam. This event occurred in the year 1610, and may be considered as the era of their sovereignty. After this event, he subdued several of the neighbouring Wadeyars, and kept them in confinement at Seringapatam. He died in the year 1617, and was succeeded by his grandson Cham Raj, who added considerably to the Mysore territories, and died in 1637. He was succeeded by a posthumous son of the former Rajah, named Immadee Raj, who, in the course of a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was poisoned by his prime minister. Canty Revy Narsa Raj, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> cousin of the deceased, was the next sovereign of Mysore. He made various conquests, and reigned till 1659. He was the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who established a mint, and coined the fanams and pagodas, still current, which go by his name. Dud Deo Raj was his successor; he made several conquests, and died in 1672. Chick Deo Raj mounted the throne in 1672, and died in 1704. This prince completed the subjugation of the turbulent landholders, made a number of prudent regulations which still exist; and, among other accessions, acquired by purchase the town and fortress of Bangalore. He also sent an embassy to the Mogul <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Aurungzebe, who conferred on him a splendid <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, and granted him permission to sit on an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> throne, which is still in existence, and was used on the late installation. Canty Raj, son of the last sovereign, mounted the throne in 1704. Having been born <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEAF_AND_DUMB">deaf and dumb</a>, he was called the Dumb Rajah. It was in this reign that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> influence of the Dulwoy, or prime minister, commenced, which ever after rendered the Rajah a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAGEANT">pageant</a>. After a nominal reign of ten years, the Dumb Rajah died, and was succeeded by Dud Kishen Raj, who left the management of affairs entirely to his ministers, and died, after an inglorious reign, in the year 1731. He was succeeded by Cham Raj, who, not having been found of a sufficiently pliable disposition, was deposed and imprisoned by his ministers, in the year 1734. On this event, the Mysore ministers deviated from the regular line of succession, and chose a boy of five years old, of another branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family, named Chick Kishen Raj, to be the pageant of their government. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of public business was at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> distributed in the offices of, 1st, Dulwoy, or commander-in-chief; 2dly, Serv Adikar, or comptroller of the revenue; and, 3dly, Purdhan, or privy counsellor. The first of these offices was held by Deo Raj, the second by Nunjeraje; but they subsequently exchanged appointments, and the influence of the latter was much increased by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to the young Rajah, in the year 1746. It was under the command of Nunjeraje Dulwoy, that a large Mysorean <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> marched to the assistance of the British, and their ally the Nabob Mohammed Aly, in the year 1758; but as the promised bribe, held out for his assistance (the cession of the fortress of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-TRICHINOPOLY">Trichinopoly</a>), was not complied with, he shortly after became their enemy, and for nearly two years laid siege to Trichinopoly; but, in the end, was compelled to abandon it, in consequence of the invasion of Mysore by an army of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a>. From this period may be dated the decline of the minister's power, the downfall of the Hindoo dynasty, and the succession of a Mahometan usurper, whose history being not generally known, it is deemed requisite to insert an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of it here. The great-grandfather and grandfather of Hyder Aly were both named Mohammed; they were <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> persons, who emigrated from the Punjab, and settled in the vicinity of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Geeso Deraz, the famous saint of Kalbergia. The son of the younger Mohammed was named Futteh Aly, who, having entered the army as a private soldier, rose by degrees to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of commander of a regiment, with the title of Naick. This person improved his fortune by marriage, but was killed in an engagement about the year 1729. Some time previous to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he had raised a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> over his father and his wife, in the vicinity of the town of Colar, and was buried there. After the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> in which Futteh Aly was killed, his family were taken prisoners, and plundered of every thing they possessed. The widow, accompanied by her two sons, Shabaz-Saheb and Hyder, boys, took refuge with her <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Ibrahim, who commanded a small body of peons or infantry, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the governor of Bangalore. When the elder brother Shabaz had attained a sufficient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, his uncle procured for him a recommendation to an officer of rank in Seringapatam; and he was received into the service as a subordinate officer of infantry, in which situation he distinguished himself, and gradually rose to the command of 200 cavalry and 1000 infantry. It is probable, that Hyder profited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> of his brother, and was employed by him in a subordinate situation; but he does not appear to have distinguished himself till the year 1749, when, during the siege of Deonhally, by his intrepidity and zeal, he attracted the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the Dulwoy Nunjeraje; and, upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, was promoted to the command of it, with a garrison of 200 infantry and 50 cavalry. Permission was also granted him to augment the number of troops, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he found it requisite. During the contest between the Nizam Nasir Jung, and his rival Muzaffir Jung, in the year 1750, Hyder Aly commanded <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the quota of Mysore troops, and distinguished himself in resisting the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>; but as soon as Nasir Jung was killed, he employed his followers in plundering the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of his late <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; and, amongst a number of other valuables, carried off two camels laden with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, 300 horses, and 500 stand of arms, all of which he conveyed safely to Deonhally. Hyder Aly was again employed at the siege of Trichinopoly; and during the battle of the 17th of August 1754, between the British and the French armies, with their allies on both sides, Hyder seeing the baggage of the British left without protection, ordered some of his troops to amuse the Tanjorine cavalry in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, whilst he with another body galloped round, and fell upon the rear of the convoy, amongst which he created great confusion, and seized 35 carts laden with ammunition and stores. On the retreat of the Mysoreans in 1755, Hyder was detached in the command of an army, consisting of 5000 infantry, 2500 cavalry, six guns, and a number of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> troops, to secure the district of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DINDIGUL">Dindigul</a>. During the three years he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the government of Dindigul, he very considerably increased the number of his troops, disciplined his battalions, and took into his service several French artificers, under whose superintendence he formed a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABORATORY">laboratory</a>, arsenal, &c. In the year 1758, a serious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> having broken out amongst the troops at Seringapatam, Hyder Aly was ordered to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> thither with all his regular corps. Partly by fair means, and partly by force, he succeeded in quelling the mutiny, and in disbanding the army; in reward for which service, he was gratified with the fortress and adjoining district of Bangalore, as a fief or personal estate. In the following year, Hyder was invested with the command of all the troops employed against the Mahrattas, and was at the same time authorized to conclude a peace with them; but as this object could not be obtained without a large sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and the government could not advance above half the amount, he was directed to borrow the remainder from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>; and in order to effect this, certain districts were assigned to him, to be held in pledge till the bankers should be reimbursed. Having appointed his own collectors to the districts, he borrowed the money, satisfied the Mahrattas, and returned in triumph to Seringapatam. His reception by the Dulwoy and young rajah was most gracious; by the former he was distinguished by the epithet of son, and by the latter honoured with the title of Behauder (the champion), which he ever after retained. In this sketch of the history of Hyder Aly, it is impossible to describe the various intrigues by which he subverted the authority of the Dulwoy (minister), and got the rajah completely into his own power. But his overweening confidence had nearly ruined him. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May 1760, Hyder Aly was induced, by the intrigues of the French, to detach to their assistance almost the whole of the regular army then at Seringapatam; whilst he continued to reside in a garden a short distance from the city, with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of only 100 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and a battalion of infantry. The rajah and his mother, a woman of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, weary of the tyranny of their oppressor, entered into a secret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with a Mahratta chief, who was encamped on the frontiers, and who agreed to send, on an appointed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, 6000 chosen horse to their assistance; but owing to the procrastination of the Mahrattas, and an ill-timed attack from the foot on the cantonment of Hyder, he effected his escape with his hundred cavalry, attended by some camels laden with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, and succeeded in reaching the fortress of Bangalore, which was garrisoned by his own troops. This event took place on the 13th of August 1760. Immediately on Hyder's entering Bangalore, he sent off an express to recall the army from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARNATIC">Carnatic</a>, under the command of his brother-in-law Mukhdum Sahib; and dispatched orders to the various detachments of his troops, dispersed over the country, to join him without loss of time. By degrees he was joined by his detachments, by new levies, by the Carnatic army, and by what was of great consequence, 200 French European cavalry, and 100 infantry, with some <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. With these forces, aided by intrigue, he defeated the Mysore troops in several engagements, and in the month of May 1761, again got possession of the person of the rajah. Hyder Aly, although now possessing all the real power of a sovereign, was still desirous of legalising his usurpation; he therefore, by means of presents or concessions, received from the Nizam of the Dekhan a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of the seminary of Mysore, with a patent constituting him a Heft Hazary, commander of 7000 horse in the imperial service, and the title of Nabob Hyder Aly Khan Behaudev. In the year 1763, he conquered the countries of Bednoor, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOONDA">Soonda</a>, and Canara; and in the three succeeding years, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CALICUT">Calicut</a>, and the greater part of Malabar. In 1766, the rajah Chick Kishen Deo died. When this circumstance was reported to Hyder, who was then at Coimbatore, he ordered the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNERAL_RITES">funeral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> to be performed with all the usual ceremonies, and directed that the eldest son of the deceased, named Nunje Raj, should be placed on the throne, with the same parade and pomp as had formerly been used for his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. Nunje Raj died, or was murdered, after a nominal reign of five years, and was succeeded by his younger brother Cham or Syama Raj, who, by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> or policy of Hyder, was installed in the same manner as his predecessor. In 1767, the Mahrattas and the Nizam, aided by a British auxiliary force, entered into an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> against Hyder Aly. They in consequence invaded Mysore, and after having taken several of the fortresses, advanced towards Seringapatam. In this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DILEMMA">dilemma</a>, Hyder ordered all the forage to be destroyed, and took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> on the banks of the river Cavery, in an entrenched camp. After some days skirmishing, Hyder contrived, by his wonderful skill in politics, not only to make peace with the Mahrattas, but to conclude an alliance with the Nizam against the British. In virtue of this treaty, the allied forces invaded the Carnatic in September; and on the 26th of that month a general engagement took place in the vicinity of Erroar. The British gained the victory, by which the Nizam, being intimidated, was glad to make peace, leaving his ally to extricate himself in the best manner he could. Hyder, much mortified by this event, commenced a regular retreat to his own country, and was pursued by the British forces under General Smith. When both armies had advanced nearly to Seringapatam, Hyder leaving his infantry and artillery to continue the retreat, wheeled off with all his cavalry, turned the rear of the British army, re-entered the Carnatic, and in a few days was at the walls of Madras. By this manoeuvre, he so intimidated the Madras government, that they were glad to make peace with him. The terms of the treaty were short and simple. All prisoners and places taken during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> were to be restored, freedom of trade was stipulated, and an offensive and defensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> concluded. In the year 1771, Mysore was invaded by a powerful army of Mahrattas, who, after defeating Hyder, advanced to, and blockaded his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>; but fortune again favoured him, by the indisposition and death of the young Peishwa, by which event dissension was sown amongst the Mahratta chiefs, and enabled Hyder to bribe them to retreat. The years 1773, 1774, 1775, and 1776, were devoted to the disciplining of his army, and to the gradual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of his territories to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west. This he was enabled to do by the dissensions of the Mahratta chiefs and the Nair princes. In 1777, Cham, or Syama, the young Mysore Rajah, died without issue. Upon this occasion, Hyder ordered eight or ten boys, lineally related to the royal family, to be brought before him, and made choice of one of them, nearly in the same manner that Ulysses discovered <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>. This boy, whose name was also Cham or Syama Raj, was the father of the present Rajah. By the treaty made with Hyder in 1769, the British had agreed to assist him against all his enemies; but when called upon to act against the Mahrattas in 1771, they had declined, and from that period Hyder harboured the most bitter hatred against them. The year 1779, when the British had quarrelled with the Mahrattas, and given offence to the Nizam, seemed a favourable opportunity of satiating his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>; he therefore, by means of his emissaries, concluded an alliance with the above mentioned powers, and invited every other sovereign in Hindostan to join the confederacy, and to make a simultaneous attack on the British territories in their respective vicinities. In conformity with this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, Hyder Aly entered the Carnatic in the month of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1780, at the head of an army consisting of 30,000 cavalry, and 40,000 infantry, with a numerous train of artillery, aided by a corps of Europeans, and a number of French officers. Hyder commanded in person the centre or main body. The left wing was under the orders of his son Tippoo Sahib, and was destined to attack the northern Circars; while the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing, under one of his most esteemed generals, penetrated into <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADURA">Madura</a> and the southern districts. During Hyder's former invasion of the Carnatic, in 1767, he had caused his army to refrain from atrocities, and to treat the prisoners with gentleness; but on this occasion he boasted, "that he was the engine of God's wrath, for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the people of the Carnatic." His army was, therefore, guilty of the greatest cruelties, laying waste the whole of the country with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; not only the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> who were taken prisoners, but the peaceable inhabitants of the villages, were driven off like flocks of sheep to Mysore. The boys were made Mahometans, and the girls disposed of as slaves. Notwithstanding Hyder was frequently defeated by the British forces under Sir Eyre Coote, his numerous cavalry and well equipped artillery enabled him to overrun the country at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and left no part of it in the possession of his enemies, except Madras, and some other fortresses. This system of warfare continued till the death of Hyder, which took place in the city of Arcot, on the morning of the 7th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1782, at the age of 64 years. At the period of Hyder's decease, his dominions, exclusive of his conquests in the Carnatic, comprehended nearly 80,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles; his territorial revenue amounted to two millions <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. Although his army consisted of 150,000 men, his treasure contained several millions in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULLION">bullion</a> and specie. Tippoo <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a>, the eldest son of Hyder, having joined the army on the 2d <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1783, quietly succeeded to the empire of his father. A feeble attempt had been made in favour of the second son, called Abd al Kereem, now a state prisoner in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>, but was considered of so little consequence, that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> never attempted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of his brother, who either was, or pretended to be deranged, and always wore the dress of a fakir, or hermit. The invasion of the western or Malabar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> by the British, and the capture of Bedenoor, compelled Tippoo to relinquish the views of his father on the Carnatic, and to proceed with all expedition to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his own territory. He left Arcot early in March; and having, in the course of the month of April, reached Bedenoor, he compelled General Matthews to capitulate. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the capitulation were, that the garrison were to pile their arms on the glacis, but to retain all their private <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>; they were then to be marched, by the shortest route, to the sea side, and thence to be embarked for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>. But Tippoo, under pretence that the public treasure had been made away with, caused all the prisoners to be plundered. They were afterwards fettered, and then dispatched to different fortresses, where most of them died through hard treatment; the general and several of the principal officers were beheaded. After this event Tippoo marched to the seaport of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANGALORE">Mangalore</a>, but was baffled in the siege of that place, till, in consequence of the peace between England and France, the French auxiliaries having declined any further co-operation with him, and the recent successes of the British in other parts of the country, compelled him to make peace. On the 11th of March 1784, a treaty was concluded between Tippoo and the British, the principal articles of which were, that all the places taken by either party during the war were to be restored, and that all the prisoners on both sides were to be released. Tippoo being now at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, employed the remainder of 1784 in the complete subjugation of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NAIRS">Nairs</a> of Malabar, and the conquest of the Coorg country. Having thus vanquished or made peace with his enemies, he returned in triumph to Seringapatam; when, feeling himself perfectly established, and his authority acknowledged, both by his subjects and the neighbouring powers, he ostentatiously mounted the throne, and assumed the title of Sultan, thereby throwing off all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to or dependence on the Rajah of Mysore or the Emperor of Hindostan; for although the name Sultan may have been given him at his birth, it certainly was never used as a title during his father's lifetime. During the years 1785, 1786, and 1787, Tippoo was engaged in hostilities against the Mahrattas and the Nizam, in which victories were gained and defeats sustained by both parties; but the general result was in favour of the Sultan. The year 1788 was occupied by Tippoo in reforming the province of Malabar, and the forcible conversion of the inhabitants to the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. In the following year he invaded the territories of the Rajah of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRAVANCORE">Travancore</a>, who being one of the British allies, applied to them for assistance, which circumstance brought on the subsequent war, at the conclusion of which, in March 1792, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Cornwallis, at the head of the allied forces, compelled Tippoo Sultan to pay the sum of four millions of money, and to relinquish the half of his dominions. In the year 1796, the Mysore Rajah Cham Raj died, leaving an only son, then two or three years old, to inherit the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his ancestors; but the haughty Sultan would not condescend to acknowledge even a nominal superior; and so far from exalting the boy to the throne of his forefathers, he barely allowed him to exist, in squalid poverty and humiliating contempt. From this period till the year 1799, Tippoo was engaged in constant intrigues with the French, and all the powers of Hindostan, in order to raise a confederacy against the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. His correspondence was detected by the Governor-general, Lord Mornington, now Marquis Wellesley. War was determined on; the British forces, with their allies, under the command of General Harris, marched to Seringapatam, and on the 4th of May 1799 put an end to the empire and life of Tippoo Sultan. It would have been no less unjust than impolitic for the British either to have taken possession of the whole of the conquered territory for themselves, or to have restored the family of Tippoo to power. It was therefore determined to place on the throne Krishna Odiaver, the son of the last Rajah, a boy of five years old; to put him in possession of the ancient capital of Mysore, with a territory surrounding it equal to that possessed by any of his ancestors, and yielding a revenue of L 1,030,000 sterling, with the entire management of the country by his own officers; but subject to the general superintendence of a British resident. On the 30th day of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1799 the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of installing the young Rajah took place, in a temporary <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> erected for the purpose in the old fortress of Mysore. It was attended by the British Commander-in-chief, by many of the principal officers of the allied forces, and by an innumerable multitude of Hindoos, who testified their most unfeigned delight on beholding a person of their own religion, the orphan of a much injured family, restored to the possessions of his ancestors. Previous to the installation pensions had been granted to most of Tippoo's officers, and the family of the Sultan were sent as state prisoners to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VELLORE">Vellore</a>, whence they were subsequently removed to Calcutta, where they now reside upon liberal allowances, and enjoy a degree of freedom much greater than would have been their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, had these events not taken place.—(<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> Gazetteer, or Geographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, Vol. IV. Part II.)

NATANTIA

Pages 878-878

Organs of Progressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">Motion</a> fitted for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">Swimming</a>. The organs of motion are situated near the anterior extremity of the body, and either consist of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> tentacula, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> membranaceous expansions. All the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> reside in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. They are nearly of the same specific gravity with the surrounding fluid, in which they float about, having their motions in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> regulated by its changes. It is however probable, that, by means of some contractile movements, they are capable of varying their density, and of rising or sinking in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. They swim slowly, even with their utmost efforts. M. Cuvier has distributed the animals of this subdivision into two classes, which he has termed Cephalopoda and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-PTEROPODA">Pteropoda</a>. I. Class.

NAUTILACEA

Pages 878-880

Furnished with a multilocular shell. This order is involved in the greatest obscurity. None of the recent <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> have been subjected to an accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, so that their connection with the order sepiaeæ may still be considered doubtful. Enough is known of the animals of two of the genera, to furnish some hints for those who are fond of classifying animals from their analogies. These genera are Spirula and Nautilus. In the Spirula, the shell, which is concealed under the skin of the back, is spiral, with the whorls separate, the mouth orbicular, the chambers perforated by a pipe, and the last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELL">cell</a> produced into a tube. The position and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this terminal tube are unknown. The S. vulgaris is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> species, and inhabits the seas in the West Indies. In the restricted genus Nautilus, the shell is supposed to be <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a>, and the body of the animal to be lodged in the last chamber, and to be fixed by a ligament which descends into the central pipe. In the shell itself, the turns of the spire are contiguous, and the last whorl embraces the others on the sides. The *N. pompilus* of Rumphius is the only species in which the animal has been detected. The other genera which have been formed in this order depend exclusively on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> furnished by the shells, and the resemblance which these bear to the preceding genera constitutes all their claim to be included in the present order. (See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a>, Genus 18, Nautilus.) II. Order. **Sepiacea.** Destitute of a multilocular shell. The sac is strengthened by horny <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> testaceous plates, unless where the habits of the animal render such support unnecessary. 1. **Head surrounded with Eight Arms and Two Feet.** The two feet are nearly similar in their structure to the arms, or tentacula, but considerably larger in their dimensions. They have their organ on the ventral side of the mouth, between that organ and the funnel. The suckers are pedunculated, with their margin strengthened by a corneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. The sac is furnished with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a>-like expansions, and strengthened internally by corneous or testaceous ribs or plates. The head is divided from the sac on all sides by a neck. The margin of the anus is surrounded with tentacula. Genus, *Sepia.*—The sac is furnished on each side throughout its whole length with a narrow fin. The suckers are irregularly scattered on the arms and feet. The back is strengthened by a complicated calcareous plate, lodged in a peculiar cavity. This plate has been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> known in the shop of the apothecary, under the name *Cuttle-fish bone,* and belongs to the species termed *S. officinalis.* Genus, *Loligo.*—Calamary. Sides of the sac only furnished partially with fins. The suckers are disposed on the arms and feet in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> row. The dorsal plate is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> and corneous, imbedded in the substance of the sac, and is multiplied with years. The *Sepia loligo* of Lin. is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a> of the genus. Dr Leach has described three new species of the genus Loligo, which were collected by Mr Cranch during the voyage to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>, in the unfortunate expedition under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Tuckey. These species belong to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> which have the suckers produced into hooked processes. In two of these species, *L. leptura* and *Smithii,* the suckers on the arms, as well as the feet, are produced into hooks; while, in one species, *L. Bankii,* the feet only are armed with hooks. The same distinguished naturalist has instituted a new genus nearly allied to Loligo, from two species collected during the same voyage. The following characters are assigned to it: "Genus, *Cranchia.*—Body oval, sack-shaped; fins approximating, their extremities free; neck with a frenum behind, connecting it with the sack, and with two other frens, connecting it with the sack before. "Sp. 1. *Cranchia scabra.*—Sack rough, with hard rough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a>. "Sp. 2. *Cranchia maculata.*—Sack smooth, beautifully mottled with distant ovate spots." **Head surrounded with Eight Arms without Feet.** The suckers have soft margins. The sac is destitute of fin-like expansions, and is either simple or strengthened in the interior by two short corneous processes. The head is united with the sac behind, without the intervention of a neck. Arms all equal in Size. Genus, *Octopus.*—Suckers arranged in a double row. The suckers are sessile. The oviduct is double. The margin of the anus is simple. The *Sepia octopodia* of Lin. is the type of the genus. Genus, *Eledona.*—Suckers on the arms disposed in a single row. M. Lamarck has figured and described two species of this genus, in the Mem. de la Soc. d'Hist. Nat. One of these is a native of the Mediterranean, and is remarkable for giving out an odour like <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>. Arms Unequal. Genus, *Ocythoe.*—Two of the arms at their inner extremities furnished with membranaceous expansions. In this genus, which was instituted by M. Rafflesque, the suckers are in a double row, and supported on footstalks. In the specimens of the *Ocythoe Cranchii,* procured during the expedition to the Congo, Dr Leach observed "four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> spots on the inside of the tube, resembling the surfaces for the secretion of mucus, two inferior and lateral, and two superior, larger, and meeting anteriorly. On the rim of the sac, immediately above the branchiae, on each side, is a small, short, fleshy tubercle, which fits into an excavation on the opposite side of the sac." Phil. Trans. 1817. This animal was long considered as the fabricator of the shell termed Argonauta or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">Paper</a> Nautilus. The observations, however, of Mr Cranch, the Zoologist to the Congo Expedition, have demonstrated that the shell is merely the temporary residence of this animal, which it quits at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. "On the 13th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>," says Dr Leach, "he placed two living specimens in a vessel of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; the animals very soon protruded their arms, and swam on and below the surface, having all the actions of the common *Polypus* (octopus) of our seas; by means of their suckers, they adhered firmly to any substance with which they came in contact, and when sticking to the sides..." of the basin, the shell might easily be withdrawn from the animal. They had the power of completely withdrawing within the shell, and of leaving it entirely. One individual quitted its shell, and lived several hours <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> about, and showing no inclination to return into it; and others left the shells as he was taking them up in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>. They changed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, like other animals of the Class Cephalopoda; when at rest the colour was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-coloured, more or less speckled with purplish; the under parts of the arms were bluish-grey; the suckers whitish." The specimens which furnished an opportunity for making the preceding observations were met with in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and afterwards on the voyage, swimming in a small argonauta, on the surface of the sea. The reader, who is desirous of farther information on this subject, may consult Dr Leach's Observations on the Genus Ocythoe of Rafinesque, and Sir E. Home on the Distinguishing Characters between the Ova of the Sepia, and those of the Vermes Testacea that Live in Water, in the Philosophical Transactions for 1817, Art. xxii. and xxiii. (both of which are added to the appendix of Captain Tuckey's Narrative), and a paper by Mr Say on the Genus Ocythoe in the Phil. Trans. 1819, Art. vii. II. Class.
